feed.title: Combined summary - A STARK proof of Bitcoin's UTXO set at block 972,500, with circuits proven in Lean

entry.title: Combined summary - A STARK proof of Bitcoin's UTXO set at block 972,500, with circuits proven in Lean
entry.summary: A recent side project has showcased the integration of STARK-based zero-knowledge proofs with Bitcoin’s consensus mechanism, yielding a cryptographic proof that verifies a substantial section of the blockchain. This demonstration, available live at [https://starknet-innovation.github.io/starked-bitcoin/](https://starknet-innovation.github.io/starked-bitcoin/) and accompanied by its source code at [https://github.com/starknet-innovation/starked-bitcoin](https://github.com/starknet-innovation/starked-bitcoin), produces a compact 1.6 MB proof file—or “seal”—that can be verified in under half a second within a standard web browser. The proof asserts three principal claims: it authenticates the entire header chain from genesis to the current tip (excluding only wall-clock time-too-new checks), thoroughly replays all transactions and block structures across blocks 935,001 through 972,500, and confirms the resulting UTXO set, matching the serialized hash provided by Bitcoin Core for this block height. Header validation encompasses stringent adherence to Bitcoin’s mainnet rules, including SHA256d linkage, proof-of-work, retargeting, and precise chainwork calculations. This is consistent with SPV-style verification, where the verifier checks cumulative chainwork against a trusted minimum. For blocks 935,001 to 972,500, every transaction is replayed, ensuring raw data matches Merkle roots, verifying both txid and wtxid, and enforcing structural correctness for transactions and blocks while tracking every coin created or spent. After processing these blocks, the UTXO set is confirmed via its hash_serialized value, which aligns with what would be produced by Core’s gettxoutsetinfo or dumptxoutset commands. To facilitate independent verification, a Merkle root is committed over the UTXO set, enabling compact inclusion or non-inclusion proofs for specific outpoints—a process supported by the online demonstration through selective segment downloads. The system currently omits script validation and signature checking, maintaining trust assumptions similar to those of assumevalid. Witness data, however, is included, paving the way for future script validation without requiring a repeat of previous computations. Replay begins from Core’s assumeUTXO snapshot at block 935,000, with all prior blocks covered solely by their headers and authenticated against the hash embedded in Core’s chain parameters. This approach mirrors the trust model adopted by assumeUTXO users, as a full-genesis proof would demand extensive computational resources—estimated at around 325 H100 GPU-hours, translating into considerable expense. The effort has not yet undergone external audit, and feedback is encouraged. Technically, the construction leverages Stwo, a circle STARKs implementation over M31, accessed through a Zig port ([https://github.com/teddyjfpender/stwo-zig](https://github.com/teddyjfpender/stwo-zig)) and equipped with a CUDA backend for byte-identical proofs. Proving large blocks with 2^23 trace rows takes under three seconds on an H100 GPU. Proofs are recursively aggregated by epoch and then combined, resulting in a unified seal binding together the header chain, block data, and UTXO set. Circuit design is conducted in Lean 4, with constraints exported for interpretation by the Zig prover. The correctness of key components—header segments, SHA-256 implementation, block validation, state transitions, and recursive composition—is ensured through machine-checked proofs. Differential fuzz testing maintains high specification fidelity by comparing Lean specifications with Bitcoin Core’s C++ codebase, covering a vast array of cases without observed mismatches. While these tests assure behavioral alignment, they do not constitute formal proofs relative to Core’s implementation. Trust is placed in the soundness of Stwo/FRI/LogUp, the Fiat–Shamir heuristic in the random oracle model (including recursive applications as discussed in [this delvingbitcoin.org thread](https://delvingbitcoin.org/t/block-wide-signature-aggregation-via-snarks/2875)), and a concise set of native verifier checks. Full documentation detailing the division between proven and trusted assumptions is maintained in [verification.md](https://github.com/starknet-innovation/starked-bitcoin/blob/a3e06f53f8b28310933265540e8b4189fe630f66/docs/reference/verification.md). A practical outcome of this research is the verify-snapshot tool, which allows anyone to independently validate an assumeUTXO snapshot using a Core dumptxoutset file and the seal. On a typical mainnet node running Core v31.1, the snapshot at block 972,500—representing more than 164 million coins and occupying 9.39 GB—was verified in seventy-two seconds while consuming just 0.5 GB of memory on an arm64 device.
